title: Contentment brings unsurpassed happiness (2.40–2.45)
hook: the fruits of the five observances, and the one Patanjali calls happiness with nothing above it

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fruits of the yamas. Around one grounded in non-harm, hostility drops away. Did you walk into a tense moment carrying nothing sharp? Day four hundred sixty-one.

A seven-year-old's birthday. For weeks there has been one gift on the list, the only thing that matters. Morning comes, the paper tears, and there it is. Pure joy. By lunchtime it's on the floor and the question has started: what can I ask for next? Nobody's a bad kid here. It's just how wanting works, at seven and at seventy. The new car, the promotion, the house with one more room. Yesterday Patanjali gave the fruits of the five restraints. Today, the fruits of the five observances. And one of them, he says, beats every gift on every list.
screen: `ONE GIFT ON THE LIST.` → `BY LUNCH: WHAT NEXT?` → `THE FRUITS OF THE OBSERVANCES.`

segments.voice: The fruits come quickly in sutras 2.40 to 2.45. From cleanliness, a certain distance from your own body, then a clear, cheerful, one-pointed mind. From discipline, the body and senses perfected as impurity burns off. From study, meeting your chosen deity. From surrender to Ishvara, the perfection of samadhi itself. But in the middle sits one line that's simpler than all the rest. Sutra 2.42: from contentment, unsurpassed happiness. Santosha. Anuttama, the word for unsurpassed, means nothing higher, nothing above it. Not the best happiness so far. The top. The classical commentary backs it up with an old verse. Whatever pleasure desire brings in this world, and whatever great pleasure there is in heaven, together they aren't worth a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes when craving ends. A sixteenth. Notice what contentment is not, in this teaching. It isn't settling. It isn't pretending you don't want anything, or that a hard situation is fine. The commentary describes it as not wanting more than what's already at hand. The ache for the next gift is what goes. The birthday child doesn't need a better gift. The gift was never the problem. The asking for the next one was. The commentary's verse places the highest happiness not at the end of getting, but at the end of wanting. It doesn't arrive. It's what's left.
screen: `THE FRUITS OF THE OBSERVANCES.` · `FROM CONTENTMENT: NOTHING HIGHER.` · `NOT WORTH A SIXTEENTH PART.` · `NOT SETTLING. THE END OF WANTING.` · then, large: `SANTOSHA.`

segments.voice: Today's practice looks for enough. Sit and let the breath settle. Notice one thing that's already here and already enough: the breath arriving without being asked, the chair holding you up, a little warmth in your hands. Stay with it. When the mind starts listing what's missing, the email, the plan, the thing you want next, notice the list, and come back to the one thing that's enough. You don't have to feel blissful. Just let enough be enough for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Contentment brings unsurpassed happiness. Sutra 2.42: from santosha, a happiness with nothing above it.
Your line: santosha. Today, the next time you catch yourself thinking I'll be happy when, finish the sentence with right now, and see if it's true. Day four hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often single out santosha as a daily practice of accepting what is at hand, and some Hindus link it to gratitude in worship, offering food to God before eating and receiving it back as a blessing.

match.prompt: each observance and its fruit — tap the pairs.

myth: contentment here means settling for less
the commentary means not wanting more than what's at hand. it isn't settling; the craving for more is what goes.
the happiness of 2.42 has nothing above it.
the commentary says desire's pleasures aren't worth a sixteenth of craving's end
an old verse quoted on 2.42 says even heaven's pleasures don't come close.

fork.setup: you finally get the thing you wanted most. by lunch you're thinking about the next one. where does Patanjali put the highest happiness?
options: in a better gift next time.
at the end of wanting more.
fork.reveal: 2.42 gives unsurpassed happiness to contentment, and the commentary puts it at the end of craving, beyond even heaven's pleasures.

original.note: Sanskrit santoṣa: contentment, satisfaction; the second niyama, whose fruit in 2.42 is unsurpassed happiness.

trapdoor: what you thought: contentment means accepting less than you deserve.
what it means: not wanting more than what's at hand, which Patanjali says brings a happiness with nothing above it.
what a scholar hears: santoshad anuttamah sukha-labhah (2.42); the commentary cites a verse that sensual and heavenly pleasures aren't worth a sixteenth of the happiness of craving's end.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 2.40–2.41, 2.43–2.45 (the fruits of cleanliness, discipline, study, surrender)
Yoga Bhashya on 2.42 (the verse of the sixteenth part)
